#### Functional PCA of subject behavioral data

All subject behavioral data were averaged over eight trial bins. We represented individual learning curves as functional data using a cubic spline basis with smoothing penalty estimated by generalized cross-validation (Härdle, 1990). We then performed functional PCA (Ramsay and Silverman, 2013), which allowed us to extract components capturing the dominant patterns of variability in subject performance. Using this analysis, we found that the top component, which describes overall learning, explained a majority of the variability (~75%) in performance. Spline smoothing and fPCA were performed using the R package fda (Ramsay et al., 2022).

### MRI acquisition

Participants were scanned using a 3-Tesla Siemens TIM MAGNETOM Trio MRI scanner located at the Centre for Neuroscience Studies, Queen’s University (Kingston, ON, Canada). Subject anatomicals were acquired using a 32-channel head coil and a T1-weighted ADNI MPRAGE sequence (TR = 1760 ms, TE = 2.98 ms, field of view = 192 mm × 240 mm × 256 mm, matrix size = 192 × 240 × 256, flip angle = 9°, 1 mm isotropic voxels). This was followed by a series of diffusion-weighted scans and a resting-state scan (which are not the focus of the present investigation). Next, we acquired fMRI volumes using a T2*-weighted single-shot gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) acquisition sequence (time to repetition [TR] = 2000 ms, slice thickness = 4 mm, in-plane resolution = 3 mm × 3 mm, time to echo [TE] = 30 ms, field of view = 240 mm × 240 mm, matrix size = 80 × 80, flip angle = 90°, and acceleration factor [integrated parallel acquisition technologies, iPAT] = 2 with generalized auto-calibrating partially parallel acquisitions [GRAPPA] reconstruction). Each volume comprised 34 contiguous (no gap) oblique slices acquired at an ~30° caudal tilt with respect to the plane of the anterior and posterior commissure (AC-PC), providing whole-brain coverage of the cerebrum and cerebellum. Note that for the current study we did not examine the changes in cerebellar activity during learning. For the baseline and learning scans, we acquired 222 and 612 imaging volumes, respectively. Each of these task-related scans included an additional six imaging volumes at both the beginning and end of the scan. On average, the total MRI scanning session lasted ~2 hrs (including setup time and image acquisition).

### fMRI preprocessing

Preprocessing of anatomical and functional MRI data was performed using fMRIPrep 20.1.1 (Esteban et al., 2019, Esteban et al., 2024; RRID:SCR_016216) which is based on Nipype 1.5.0 (Gorgolewski et al., 2011; Gorgolewski et al., 2018; RRID:SCR_002502). Many internal operations of fMRIPrep use Nilearn 0.6.2 (Abraham et al., 2014; RRID:SCR_001362), mostly within the functional processing workflow. For more details of the pipeline, see the section corresponding to workflows in fMRIPrep’s documentation. Below we provide a condensed description of the preprocessing steps.

T1w images were corrected for intensity non-uniformity (INU) with N4BiasFieldCorrection (Tustison et al., 2010), distributed with ANTs 2.2.0 (Avants et al., 2008; RRID:SCR_004757). The T1w-reference was then skull-stripped with a Nipype implementation of the antsBrainExtraction.sh workflow (from ANTs), using OASIS30ANTs as target template. Brain tissue segmentation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), white matter (WM), and gray matter (GM) was performed on the brain-extracted T1w using fast (FSL 5.0.9, RRID:SCR_002823)(Zhang et al., 2001). A T1w-reference map was computed after registration of the T1w images (after INU-correction) using mri_robust_template (FreeSurfer 6.0.1; Reuter et al., 2010). Brain surfaces were reconstructed using recon-all (FreeSurfer 6.0.1, RRID:SCR_001847; Dale et al., 1999), and the brain mask estimated previously was refined with a custom variation of the method to reconcile ANTs-derived and FreeSurfer-derived segmentations of the cortical gray-matter of Mindboggle (RRID:SCR_002438; Klein et al., 2017). Volume-based spatial normalization to standard space (MNI152NLin6Asym) was performed through nonlinear registration with antsRegistration (ANTs 2.2.0), using brain-extracted versions of both T1w reference and the T1w template.

For each BOLD run, the following preprocessing was performed. First, a reference volume and its skull-stripped version were generated using a custom methodology of fMRIPrep. Head-motion parameters with respect to the BOLD reference (transformation matrices, and six corresponding rotation and translation parameters) are estimated before any spatiotemporal filtering using mcflirt (FSL 5.0.9; Jenkinson et al., 2002). BOLD runs were slice-time corrected using 3dTshift from AFNI 20160207 (Cox and Hyde, 1997; RRID:SCR_005927). The BOLD reference was then co-registered to the T1w reference using bbregister (FreeSurfer) which implements boundary-based registration (Greve and Fischl, 2009). Co-registration was configured with six degrees of freedom. The BOLD time series were resampled with a single interpolation step by composing all the pertinent transformations (i.e. head-motion transform matrices, and co-registrations to anatomical and output spaces). BOLD time series were resampled onto their original, native space, as well as standard space (MNI152NLin6Asym), using antsApplyTransforms (ANTs), configured with Lanczos interpolation to minimize the smoothing effects of other kernels (Lanczos, 1964). Striatal data in standard space was combined with resampled BOLD time series on the fsaverage surface to produce Grayordinates files (Glasser et al., 2013) containing 91k samples, using fsaverage as the intermediate standardized surface space. Resampling onto fsaverage was performed using mri_vol2surf (FreeSurfer).

A set of 34 motion and physiological regressors were extracted in order to mitigate the impact of head motion and physiological noise. The six head-motion estimates calculated in the correction step were expanded to include temporal derivatives and quadratic terms of each of the original and derivative regressors, totaling 24 head-motion parameters (Satterthwaite et al., 2013). Ten component-based physiological regressors were estimated using the aCompCor approach (Behzadi et al., 2007; Muschelli et al., 2014), where the top five PCs were separately extracted from WM and CSF masks. PCs were estimated after high-pass filtering the preprocessed BOLD time series (using a discrete cosine filter with 128 s cut-off).

#### Regional time-series extraction

For each participant and scan, the average BOLD time series were computed from the grayordinate time series for (1) each of the 998 regions defined according to the Schaefer 1000 parcellation (Schaefer et al., 2018; two regions are removed from the parcellation due to their small parcel size) and (2) each of the 12 striatal regions defined according to the Harvard-Oxford atlas (Frazier et al., 2005; Makris et al., 2006), which included the caudate, putamen, accumbens, pallidum, hippocampus, and amygdala. Region time series were denoised using the above-mentioned confound regressors in conjunction with the discrete cosine regressors (128 s cut-off for high-pass filtering) produced from fMRIprep and low-pass filtering using a Butterworth filter (100 s cut-off) implemented in Nilearn. Finally, all region time series were z-scored.

### Neuroimaging data analysis

#### Covariance estimation and centering

For every participant, region time series from the task scans were spliced into three equal-lengthed task epochs (210 imaging volumes each), after having discarded the first six imaging volumes (thus avoiding scanner equilibrium effects). This allowed us to estimate functional connectivity from continuous brain activity over the corresponding 70 trials for each epoch; Baseline comprised of the initial 70 trials in which subjects performed the motor task in the absence of any reward feedback, whereas the early and late learning epochs consisted of the first and last 70 trials after the onset of reward feedback, respectively. Then, we separately estimated functional connectivity matrices for each epoch by computing the region-wise covariance matrices using the Ledoit–Wolf estimator (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004). Note that our use of equal-length epochs for the three phases ensured that no biases in covariance estimation were introduced due to differences in time-series length.

Next, we centered the connectivity matrices using the approach advocated by Zhao et al., 2018, which leverages the natural geometry of the space of covariance matrices (Areshenkoff et al., 2022; Areshenkoff et al., 2021). In brief, this involved adjusting the covariance matrices of each participant to have a common mean, which was equivalent to the overall mean covariance, thus removing subject-specific variations in functional connectivity. First, a grand mean covariance matrix, $S-_{gm}$ , was computed by taking the geometric mean covariance matrix across all $i$ participants and $j$ epochs. Then, for each participant we computed the geometric mean covariance matrix across task epochs, $S-_{i}$ , and each task epoch covariance matrix $S_{ij}$ was projected onto the tangent space at this mean participant covariance matrix $S_{i}$ to obtain a tangent vector

$$
T_{ij}=S-_{i}^{1/2}log⁡S-_{i}^{-1/2}S_{ij}S-_{i}^{-1/2}S-_{i}^{1/2}
$$

where log denotes the matrix logarithm. We then transported each tangent vector to the grand mean $S-_{gm}$ using the transport proposed by Zhao et al., 2018, obtaining a centered tangent vector

$$
T_{ij}^{c}=GT_{ij}G^{⊤}
$$

where $G=S-_{gm}^{1/2}S_{i}^{-1/2}$ . This centered tangent vector now encodes the same difference in covariance, but now expressed relative to the grand mean. Finally, we projected each centered tangent vector back onto the space of covariance matrices, to obtain the centered covariance matrix

$$
S_{ij}^{c}=S-_{gm}^{1/2}exp⁡S-_{gm}^{-1/2}T_{ij}^{c}S-_{gm}^{-1/2}S-_{gm}^{1/2}
$$

where $exp$ denotes the matrix exponential. For the benefits of this centering approach, see Figure 2, and for an additional overview, see Areshenkoff et al., 2022.

Note that we have implemented many of the computations required to replicate the analysis in an publicly available R package spdm, which is freely available from GitHub (Areshenkoff, 2023).

#### Manifold construction

Connectivity manifolds for all centered functional connectivity matrices were derived in the following steps. First, consistent with previous studies (Gale et al., 2022; Hong et al., 2020; Margulies et al., 2016; Vos de Wael et al., 2020), we applied row-wise thresholding to retain the top 10% connections in each row, and then computed cosine similarity between each row to produce an affinity matrix that describes the similarity of each region’s connectivity profiles. Second, we applied PCA to obtain a set of PCs that provide a low-dimensional representation of connectivity structure (i.e., connectivity gradients). We selected PCA as our dimension reduction technique based on recent work demonstrating the improved reliability of PCA over nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., diffusion map embedding; Hong et al., 2020).

To provide a basis for comparing changes in functional network architecture that arise during learning specifically, we constructed a template manifold using the same aforementioned manifold construction procedures from a group-average baseline connectivity matrix that was derived from the geometric mean (across participants) of all centered baseline connectivity matrices. We aligned all individual manifolds (36 participants × 3 epochs; 108 total) to this baseline template manifold using Procrustes alignment. All analyses on the aligned manifolds were performed using the top three PCs, which cumulatively explained ~70% of the total variance in the template manifold. Across participants and epochs, the top three PCs, following Procrustes alignment, had an average correlation of r = 0.88 with their respective PCs in the template manifold, thus demonstrating good overall reliability and alignment across participants and epochs. Together, this approach enabled us to uniquely examine the learning-related changes in manifold structure (during early and late learning), and specifically how these deviate from the baseline task functional architecture.

#### Manifold eccentricity and analyses

Recent work has quantified the embedding of regions and networks in low-dimensional spaces using Euclidean distance as a measure (Bethlehem et al., 2020; Park et al., 2021a; Park et al., 2021b; Valk et al., 2023). ‘Eccentricity’ refers to the Euclidean distance between a single region and the manifold centroid (Park et al., 2021a), which, in the case of PCA, is equivalent to a region’s magnitude, or vector length. Note that eccentricity provides a scalar index of network integration and segregation, in which distal regions with greater eccentricity are more segregated than proximal regions that integrate more broadly across functional networks (Park et al., 2021a; Park et al., 2021b; Valk et al., 2023). To validate this interpretation with our own data, we correlated the baseline template manifold eccentricity with three graph theoretical measures of functional integration and segregation. These measures were calculated on the row-wise thresholded template connectivity matrix and included node strength, which is the sum of a region’s connectivity weights; within-module degree z-score, which measures the degree centrality of a region within its respective network; and participation coefficient, which measures the network diversity of a region’s connectivity distribution (Rubinov and Sporns, 2010). Regions were assigned to their respective intrinsic functional networks (Schaefer et al., 2018; Thomas Yeo et al., 2011) for calculations of within-module degree z-score and participation coefficient.

We computed eccentricity for each brain region for all individual manifolds (each participant and epoch). This allowed us to observe manifold expansions (increases in eccentricity) and contractions (decreases in eccentricity) throughout early and late learning, thereby probing learning-related changes in functional segregation and integration (e.g., see Figure 4). We compared region eccentricity between the baseline, early, and late learning epochs by performing a series of region-wise paired t-tests between these three key epochs. We applied FDR correction (q < 0.05) across regions for each contrast.

#### Seed connectivity analyses

In order to understand the underlying changes in regional covariance that ultimately give rise to the observed changes in manifold eccentricity, we performed seed connectivity contrasts between the different task epochs. To this end, we selected several seed regions that were statistically significant in the early learning > baseline contrast, which included areas in the left MPFC, left premotor cortex (PMd), and left PMC, thereby allowing us to characterize some of the cortical and striatal changes that are associated reward-based learning. For completeness, we also selected homologous regions in the right hemisphere (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1). For each seed region, we generated functional connectivity maps for the epochs of interest in every participant and computed region-wise paired t-tests for both the early > baseline and late > early contrasts. For all contrasts, we opted to show the unthresholded t-maps so as to visualize the complete multivariate pattern of connectivity changes that drive changes in eccentricity (a multivariate measure). In addition, we constructed spider plots further characterizing these changes at the network level by averaging the t-values across individual regions according to their network assignment (Thomas Yeo et al., 2011). Note that these analyses are mainly intended to provide characterization (and interpretation) of the connectivity changes of representative regions from our main eccentricity analyses.

#### Behavioral correlation analyses

To investigate the relationship between changes in manifold structure and individual differences in learning performance, we computed a correlation, across participants, between learning score and each region’s change in eccentricity from baseline to early learning (Figure 6C) and from early to late learning (Figure 6D). This produced two correlation maps, one for each contrast. We found that the spatial specificity of significant regions in these correlation maps overlapped substantially with the dorsal attention A (DAN-A) network, from the 17-network Schaefer 1000 assignments (Schaefer et al., 2018). This was determined by evaluating the mean correlation (across regions) for each of the 17-network assignments against a null distribution generated by projecting each brain region’s correlation onto their respective Schaefer 1000 parcels on the 32k fsLR spherical mesh and performing 1000 iterations of the Váša spin-testing permutation procedure (Markello et al., 2022; Váša et al., 2018). This allowed us to generate, for each brain network and pairwise comparison (baseline to early learning and early to late learning), a topographical distribution of correlations that could be expected simply due to chance from spatial autocorrelations in the brain maps (see Figure 6E and F). We then empirically assessed the statistical significance of our real correlation values against this spatial null distribution for each brain network. Because the spin-testing procedure assesses only the probability of having observed a given correlation value, and not whether that correlation value itself differs from zero, we incorporated the additional stipulation that an effect would be deemed significant only if the real correlation value was also statistically different from zero (at p<0.05).

To explore the underlying changes in functional connectivity that give way to these brain–behavior correlations, we performed seed connectivity contrasts, using paired t-tests on the 17-network parcellation, between the different task epochs (early > baseline and late > early). As with the ‘Seed connectivity analyses’ section above, we opted to show the unthresholded t-maps so as to visualize the complete multivariate pattern of connectivity that underlies the brain–behavior correlations (Figure 6G). Together, these complementary approaches enabled us to explore how individual differences in performance relate to changes in manifold structure at the region- and network levels.

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.91928.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.91928.3.sa3)

Summary:

The manuscript of Nick and colleagues addresses the intriguing question of how brain connectivity evolves during reward-based motor learning. The concept of quantifying connectivity through changes in extraction and contraction across lower-dimensional manifolds is both novel and interesting and the presented results are clear and well-presented. Overall, the manuscript is a valuable addition to the field.

Strengths:

This manuscript is written in a clear and comprehensible way. It introduces a rather novel technique of assessing connectivity across lower-dimensional manifold which has hitherto not been applied in this way to the question of reward-based motor learning. Thus, this presents a unique viewpoint on understanding how the brain changes with motor learning. I particularly enjoyed the combination of connectivity-based, followed by further scrutiny of seed-based connectivity analyses, thus providing a more comprehensive viewpoint. Now it also has added a more comprehensive report on the behavioural changes of learning, and the added statistical quantification, which is useful.

Weaknesses:

The main weakness of the manuscript is the lack of direct connection between the reported neural changes and behavioural learning. Namely, most of the results could also be explained by changes in attention allocation during the session, or changes in movement speed (independent of learning). The authors acknowledge some of these potential confounds and argue that factors like attention are important for learning. While this is true, it is nonetheless very limiting if one cannot ascertain whether the observed effects are due to attention (independent of learning) or attention allocated in the pursuit of learning. The only direct analysis linking behavioural changes to neural changes is based on individual differences in learning performance, where the DAN-A shows the opposite trend than group level effects, which they interpret as differences given the used higher-resolution parcellation. However, it could be that these learning effects are indeed much smaller and subtler compared to more dominant group-level attention effects during the task. The lack of a control condition in the task limits the interpretability of results as learning-related.

claims.evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The default mode network (DMN) was initially identified through its tendency to deactivate during cognitively demanding tasks.
claims.source: Initially identified through its tendency to deactivate during cognitively demanding tasks, the DMN has traditionally been implicated in largely introspective, abstract cognitive functions such as autobiographical memory and internal mentation (Andrews‐Hanna et al., 2014; Binder et al., 2009; Christoff et al., 2016; Schacter et al., 2012; Spreng et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Directly stated historical characterization with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Areas of the DMN are activated during demanding decision-making and working-memory tasks.
claims.source: In recent years, however, this characterization of DMN activity has been difficult to reconcile, with an emerging body of functional MRI (fMRI) and neurophysiological evidence showing that areas of this network are activated during demanding decision-making and working-memory tasks (Foster et al., 2023; Hayden et al., 2009; Heilbronner and Platt, 2013; Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018; Pearson et al., 2009; Vatansever et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Each core region of the DMN is located in regions of association cortex that are equidistant between different primary systems.
claims.source: One hypothesis concerning this system's function pertains to its unique topographic positioning on the cortical mantle (Smallwood et al., 2021): Each core region of the DMN is located in regions of association cortex that are equidistant between different primary systems
claims.evidence: Directly stated hypothesis with citation.

claims.claim: Posteromedial cortex, a key node of the DMN, is located precisely at the midpoint between the calcarine (visual) and central (motor) sulci.

claims.evidence: Directly stated anatomical fact with citation.

claims.claim: The unique topographic location of DMN regions is hypothesized to allow them broad oversight over distributed brain functions, enabling them to play a role in the coordination of activity across cortex.
claims.source: This unique topographic location is hypothesized to allow DMN regions broad oversight over distributed brain functions, enabling them to play a role in the coordination of activity across cortex (Smallwood et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Directly stated hypothesis with citation.

claims.claim: DMN areas such as medial frontal cortex and posteromedial cortex appear to play an important role in shifting between information gathering versus information exploitation during reward-guided decision-making tasks.
claims.source: For instance, DMN areas such as medial frontal cortex and posteromedial cortex appear to play an important role in shifting between information gathering versus information exploitation during reward-guided decision-making tasks (Barack et al., 2017; Foster et al., 2023; Pearson et al., 2011; Pearson et al., 2009; Schuck et al., 2015; Trudel et al., 2021)—the so-called explore/exploit trade-off (Frank et al., 2009; Sutton and Barto, 2018).
claims.evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The DMN supports behavior under conditions in which performance depends on knowledge accrued across several trials rather than by immediate sensory inputs.
claims.source: Consistent with this, recent studies have argued that broad features of the DMN's activity can be explained under the auspices that it supports behavior under conditions in which performance depends on knowledge accrued across several trials rather than by immediate sensory inputs (Hayden et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018; Vatansever et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claims.evidence: Directly stated prior finding with citation.

claims.claim: High-dimensional neural population activity can be described along a low-dimensional subspace or manifold.

claims.source: This same organizational structure also appears to govern the macroscale activity of cortex, with this manifold approach having recently provided key insights into the overarching structural and functional architecture of the human brain (Huntenburg et al., 2018; Paquola et al., 2019; Shine et al., 2019a; Shine et al., 2019b; Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019).

results.result: The study recruited 46 right-handed participants (27 females, aged 18–28 years), excluded 10 due to data quality issues, resulting in a final sample of 36 participants. The study received ethics approval from Queen's University Research Ethics Board (CNS-019-16).
results.evaluation: Claims C1–C4 provide complete and consistent information about participant recruitment, exclusion criteria, final sample size, and ethics approval. The arithmetic is correct (46-10=36), exclusion criteria are clearly defined, and ethics approval is documented.

results.result: Participants performed a reward-based motor learning task with a baseline block (70 trials, no feedback) followed by a learning block (200 trials with score feedback). The task design isolated reward-based learning by eliminating visual feedback of finger trajectories, preventing error-based learning. Participants successfully increased their scores over the 200 learning trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C5–C11 describe the experimental design and behavioral results. The task structure is clearly defined with appropriate controls. The claim that only reward-based learning was possible (C8) is supported by the experimental design (no visual feedback), though the complete elimination of error-based learning is a strong assumption. Behavioral improvement (C10) is supported by Figure 1D.

results.result: BOLD time-series data were extracted using the Schaefer 1000 cortical parcellation and Harvard-Oxford striatal parcellation, and functional connectivity matrices were estimated for each epoch. A Riemannian manifold centering procedure was applied to remove subject-level variance, which successfully abolished subject-level clustering and revealed task-related structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C12–C18 describe the data extraction and preprocessing pipeline. The methods are well-documented with appropriate citations. The effectiveness of the centering procedure is demonstrated in Figure 2, showing clear abolishment of subject-level clustering. The rationale for centering (C15) is supported by multiple citations.

results.result: The top three principal components of the baseline manifold explain approximately 70% of variance and recapitulate the tripartite structure of brain organization, distinguishing visual, somatomotor, and default mode network regions along a processing hierarchy from unimodal to transmodal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C19–C24 describe the baseline manifold structure. The quantitative result (70% variance explained) is clearly stated with figure reference. The interpretation of PCs replicating known brain architecture is supported by citations and consistent with prior literature. The tripartite structure is well-established in the field.

results.result: Manifold eccentricity, computed as Euclidean distance from the manifold centroid, provides a measure of functional segregation versus integration. This interpretation is validated by strong correlations with graph-theoretic measures: positive correlations with node strength (r=0.88) and within-module degree (r=0.45), and negative correlation with participation coefficient (r=-0.74).
results.evaluation: Claims C25–C29 define the eccentricity metric and validate its interpretation. The validation approach is sound, using established graph-theoretic measures. All correlations are statistically significant (p<0.001) and show expected patterns. The strong correlation with node strength (r=0.88) particularly supports the interpretation.

results.result: During early learning (baseline to early contrast), most brain regions showed manifold expansion (increased segregation), including sensorimotor areas, DAN regions, and DMN areas. However, posterior medial cortex and posterior angular gyrus showed manifold contraction (increased integration). No significant changes were observed in striatal regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C34–C38 describe the primary findings for early learning. The results are supported by Figure 4A with appropriate statistical correction (FDR q<0.05). The null result for striatum (C38) is appropriately reported. The pattern of expansion and contraction is clearly documented across multiple brain regions.

results.result: During late learning (early to late contrast), the pattern reversed: DMN regions showed contraction while PMC and posterior AG showed expansion. Salience/ventral attention network regions also showed expansion. Again, no significant striatal changes were observed, though right pallidum approached significance (p=0.01) but did not survive FDR correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C39–C43 describe late learning changes. The reversal pattern is clearly documented in Figure 4B. The null result for striatum is consistently reported with appropriate statistical detail (C43). The near-significant result for right pallidum is appropriately disclosed with exact p-value and corrected alpha threshold.

results.result: Seed connectivity analysis of left MPFC revealed that its manifold expansion during early learning arose from increased within-DMN connectivity (segregation), while its contraction during late learning arose from increased connectivity with DAN sensorimotor areas (integration).
results.evaluation: Claims C44–C47 provide mechanistic interpretation of MPFC eccentricity changes through seed connectivity analysis. The connectivity patterns (C44, C45) are supported by Figure 5A. The interpretations (C46, C47) logically follow from the connectivity data and are consistent with the eccentricity framework established earlier.

results.result: Left premotor cortex (PMd) showed increased connectivity with DAN and SalVentAttn networks and decreased connectivity with DMN during early learning, with this pattern reversing during late learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C48–C50 describe PMd connectivity changes supported by Figure 5B. The pattern is inverse to MPFC, showing sensorimotor regions coupling with attention networks early and DMN late. The reversal pattern strengthens the overall interpretation of network reconfiguration during learning.

results.result: Left posterior medial cortex (PMC) showed a unique pattern opposite to other regions: decreased within-DMN connectivity and increased connectivity with DAN and SalVentAttn during early learning (manifold contraction), reversing to increased within-DMN connectivity during late learning (manifold expansion).
results.evaluation: Claims C51–C55 describe PMC's distinctive connectivity pattern supported by Figure 5C. The opposite pattern compared to other DMN regions is clearly documented. The interpretations (C54, C55) are consistent with the eccentricity framework and suggest a special coordinating role for PMC.

results.result: The study identifies a general pattern of network reconfiguration during learning: DAN sensorimotor areas couple with SalVentAttn network during early learning and switch to DMN coupling during late learning. Posteromedial cortex shows the opposite pattern, suggesting a coordinating role.
results.evaluation: Claims C30–C33, C56–C57 synthesize the main findings. The pattern is consistently supported across multiple analyses (whole-brain eccentricity, seed connectivity). The interpretation of PMC's coordinating role (C33) is speculative but reasonable given its unique pattern. This represents the core finding of the manuscript.

results.result: Subjects showed significant individual variation in motor learning ability. Functional PCA identified a single component capturing approximately 75% of variability in learning curves, providing a scalar measure of overall learning performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C58–C60 describe the behavioral analysis approach. The use of fPCA is appropriate for capturing temporal patterns in learning curves. The 75% variance explained indicates a dominant pattern of individual differences. The method is well-justified and properly implemented.

results.result: Changes in DAN-A network eccentricity correlated with learning performance: greater contraction during early learning and greater expansion during late learning predicted better performance. This was driven by DAN-A connectivity with SalVentAttn-B during early learning and DMN-B during late learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C61–C65 describe brain-behavior relationships supported by Figure 7. The statistical approach using spin-test permutation with spatial autocorrelation correction is rigorous. The specificity to DAN-A (not DAN-B) is appropriately documented. The connectivity patterns (C63, C64) provide mechanistic insight into the performance relationship.

results.result: No significant changes in striatal regions were observed during learning. The authors suggest this may reflect methodological limitations (coarse parcellation, small striatal size) rather than absence of striatal involvement, noting that cortical manifold structure was largely independent of striatal inclusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C42–C43, C92–C94 address the null striatal findings. The null results are appropriately reported with statistical details. The methodological limitations are thoughtfully discussed (C92, C93). The independence of cortical manifold from striatal inclusion (C94, Figure 3—supplement 2) supports the validity of the cortical findings despite the null striatal results.

results.result: fMRI data were preprocessed using fMRIPrep 20.1.1 with standard procedures including motion correction, slice-timing correction, coregistration, spatial normalization, and denoising with 34 motion and physiological regressors. Time series were filtered (high-pass 128s, low-pass 100s) and z-scored.
results.evaluation: Claims C95–C109 document the preprocessing pipeline. The use of fMRIPrep is standard and appropriate. All preprocessing steps are clearly described with software versions and parameters. The 34-regressor denoising approach (24 motion + 10 aCompCor) is rigorous. The filtering parameters are reasonable for fMRI data.

results.result: Functional connectivity matrices were estimated using Ledoit-Wolf estimator with equal-length epochs to avoid bias. Manifolds were constructed using PCA (selected for reliability over nonlinear methods) with row-wise thresholding (top 10%) and cosine similarity. Individual manifolds were aligned to baseline template using Procrustes alignment (average r=0.88). Statistical comparisons used FDR correction (q<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C110–C116 describe the manifold construction and statistical methods. The Ledoit-Wolf estimator is appropriate for high-dimensional covariance estimation. The choice of PCA over nonlinear methods is justified by citation (C113). The Procrustes alignment quality (r=0.88) indicates good reliability. Statistical correction is appropriate.

results.result: Network-level correlations with behavior were tested using spatial autocorrelation-preserving null models (spin-test) to account for spatial structure in brain maps.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 describes the statistical approach for brain-behavior correlations. The spin-test method is state-of-the-art for controlling spatial autocorrelation in brain maps. The approach is properly cited and appropriately applied to network-level analyses.

results.result: The introduction establishes that MPFC and striatum evaluate prediction errors for learning, that DMN was historically associated with task-negative activity but is now recognized to support demanding cognitive tasks, and that DMN's unique topographic position may enable coordination of distributed brain functions. Prior work showed DMN involvement in motor adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C66–C75 provide background context from prior literature. All claims are supported by appropriate citations. The characterization of DMN's evolving understanding (C68, C69) accurately reflects the literature. The topographic hypothesis (C70–C72) is properly attributed. The prior motor adaptation finding (C75) provides direct motivation for the current study.

results.result: The manifold approach, originally developed for neural population activity in macaques, has been successfully applied to human brain organization. SalVentAttn network regions are implicated in cognitive control, motivation, exploratory behavior, and responding to novel stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C76–C81 provide methodological and theoretical background. The manifold approach's origins and applications are properly cited (C76, C77). The characterization of SalVentAttn function (C78–C81) is supported by appropriate citations and provides context for interpreting the results.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within prior literature showing that early reward-guided learning involves more variable, exploratory behavior, and that DMN-premotor connectivity increases after rule learning. The results support the hypothesis that DMN-sensorimotor interactions enable memory-guided behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C82–C85 interpret the results in light of prior work. The connections to prior literature are appropriate and well-cited. The interpretation that DMN supports memory-guided behavior (C85) is consistent with the data showing late-learning DMN-sensorimotor coupling, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The discussion proposes that PMC's unique properties—containing signals from across cortex, linked to reward processing and strategy selection, and capable of long-timescale integration—position it to orchestrate the transition from exploration to exploitation during learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C86–C91 propose a specific functional role for PMC. While the properties attributed to PMC (C86–C89) are supported by citations, the proposed orchestrating role (C90, C91) is speculative. The data show PMC's unique connectivity pattern but do not directly test its causal role in coordinating network transitions. This interpretation, while plausible, requires additional evidence.

results.result: The study establishes neural changes supporting reward-based motor learning and identifies distinct transitions in functional coupling between sensorimotor and transmodal cortex during behavioral adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C118–C119 state the main conclusions. These are well-supported by the comprehensive set of analyses showing systematic changes in network organization during learning. The identification of distinct early and late learning patterns with reversal of connectivity is a robust finding replicated across multiple analytical approaches.

results.result: The study recruited 46 right-handed participants (27 females, aged 18–28 years), excluded 10 due to data quality issues, and analyzed data from 36 participants with appropriate ethics approval.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the sample size, exclusion criteria, or ethics approval. The methodological details are treated as standard and acceptable for this type of neuroimaging study.

results.result: Participants performed a baseline block (70 trials, no feedback) followed by a learning block (200 trials with reward feedback). The task design isolated reward-based learning by withholding visual feedback about finger trajectory, preventing error-based learning. Subjects successfully increased their scores over the 200 learning trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers described the task as 'novel,' 'compelling,' and 'goes beyond the current state of the art.' One reviewer noted the task is 'new' and represents a methodological advance. The behavioral learning effect is accepted without challenge.

results.result: The study defined three equal-length epochs (baseline, early learning, late learning) and extracted BOLD time-series from cortical (Schaefer 1000) and striatal (Harvard-Oxford) parcellations. Covariance matrices were estimated for each epoch and centered using a Riemannian manifold approach to remove subject-level clustering and reveal task-related effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the 'state-of-the-art neuroimaging analyses' and 'interesting analysis approaches.' The centering procedure and manifold approach are treated as methodologically sound and appropriate for isolating task-related connectivity changes.

results.result: The top three principal components of the baseline manifold explain ~70% of variance and replicate the tripartite structure of brain organization: PC1 distinguishes visual from somatomotor regions, PC2 distinguishes visual/somatomotor from DMN regions, and PC3 represents a gradient of DAN/FCN versus DMN regions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the PCA results or the interpretation of the tripartite structure. The manifold approach is described as 'novel' and 'interesting,' and the baseline characterization is treated as a valid foundation for subsequent analyses.

results.result: Manifold eccentricity (Euclidean distance from centroid) was computed for each region and interpreted as reflecting functional segregation (higher eccentricity) versus integration (lower eccentricity). Baseline eccentricity correlates positively with node strength (r=0.88) and within-manifold degree (r=0.45), and negatively with participation coefficient (r=−0.74).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the eccentricity metric or its interpretation. The correlations with standard graph-theoretic measures are presented as validation, and reviewers accepted this framework for interpreting connectivity changes.

results.result: During early learning, sensorimotor areas in the dorsal attention network showed increased covariance with salience/ventral attention network areas and reduced covariance with DMN areas. During late learning, this pattern reversed, with sensorimotor areas showing increased covariance with DMN areas. Posteromedial cortex showed the opposite pattern across learning phases.
results.evaluation: While reviewers described the findings as 'clear and well-presented,' one reviewer raised a critical concern: 'most of the results could also be explained by changes in attention allocation during the session, or changes in movement speed (independent of learning).' The lack of a control condition limits interpretability as learning-specific versus generic task engagement effects.

results.result: From baseline to early learning, several brain regions exhibited manifold expansion (increased eccentricity/segregation), including bilateral sensorimotor, premotor, supplementary motor, superior parietal cortex, lateral visual cortex, and DMN areas (MFG, MPFC, IFG, MTC). In contrast, posterior medial cortex (PMC) and posterior angular gyrus exhibited manifold contraction (decreased eccentricity/integration).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the results are 'clear' but expressed concern about whether these changes reflect learning-specific processes or generic attention/engagement effects. One reviewer noted 'it is nonetheless very limiting if one cannot ascertain whether the observed effects are due to attention (independent of learning) or attention allocated in the pursuit of learning.'

results.result: No significant changes in striatal regions were observed from baseline to early learning or from early to late learning. The right pallidum approached significance (p=0.01) but did not survive FDR correction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the null findings in the striatum. The authors' discussion of potential methodological limitations (parcellation resolution) is treated as reasonable speculation rather than a fundamental flaw.

results.result: From early to late learning, DMN regions (MFG, MPFC, IFG, MTC) exhibited manifold contraction (increased integration), while PMC and posterior angular gyrus exhibited manifold expansion (increased segregation). Salience/ventral attention network areas (dACC, anterior insula) also showed expansion during late learning.
results.evaluation: Similar to early learning effects, reviewers questioned whether these changes are learning-specific or reflect generic task engagement dynamics. The reversal pattern is noted but its interpretation as learning-related remains uncertain without a control condition.

results.result: Seed-based connectivity analysis of left MPFC showed that during early learning, MPFC increased connectivity with other DMN regions and decreased connectivity with DAN areas. During late learning, this pattern reversed. The authors interpret manifold expansion of MPFC during early learning as arising from DMN segregation, and contraction during late learning as arising from increased connectivity with DAN areas.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the 'combination of connectivity-based, followed by further scrutiny of seed-based connectivity analyses' as providing 'a more comprehensive viewpoint.' However, the concern about learning-specificity versus attention effects applies equally to these seed-based results.

results.result: During early learning, left premotor cortex (PMd) increased connectivity with DAN and salience/ventral attention network areas, and decreased connectivity with DMN areas and hippocampus. During late learning, this pattern reversed, with increased DMN/hippocampus connectivity and decreased DAN/salience connectivity.
results.evaluation: The seed-based analysis is methodologically sound and complements the manifold findings, but the interpretation as learning-specific remains uncertain due to the lack of control for generic attention or engagement effects.

results.result: During early learning, left PMC decreased connectivity with other DMN-A and Control-C regions, hippocampus, and MPFC, while increasing connectivity with DAN and salience/ventral attention areas. During late learning, this reversed. The authors interpret PMC contraction during early learning as arising from integration with DAN/salience networks, and expansion during late learning as arising from within-network DMN/Control segregation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted the PMC findings as interesting and the opposite pattern compared to other regions is acknowledged. However, the learning-specificity concern applies here as well, and the interpretation of PMC as orchestrating explore/exploit transitions remains speculative.

results.result: Summary finding: During early learning, there is increased functional coupling between DAN sensorimotor areas and salience/ventral attention network areas. During late learning, DAN sensorimotor areas switch their connectivity to DMN areas.
results.evaluation: This is the core summary result of the paper. While reviewers found it 'clear and well-presented,' the critical limitation is that 'it remains to be seen whether these changes reflect generic changes in task engagement during learning or are specific to reward-based motor learning.'

results.result: Individual differences analysis: Subjects exhibit significant variation in motor learning ability. Functional PCA identified a single component capturing ~75% of learning curve variability. The change in eccentricity of the DAN-A network correlated with learning performance: greater contraction from baseline to early learning and greater expansion from early to late learning were associated with better task performance.
results.evaluation: One reviewer noted this is 'the only direct analysis linking behavioural changes to neural changes' but expressed concern that 'the DAN-A shows the opposite trend than group level effects.' The reviewer suggests 'it could be that these learning effects are indeed much smaller and subtler compared to more dominant group-level attention effects during the task.'

results.result: During early learning, DAN-A regions showed largest connectivity increases with salience/ventral attention subnetwork (SalVentAttn-B). During late learning, DAN-A regions showed largest connectivity increases with DMN subnetwork (DMN-B). This transition in functional coupling is associated with differences in subject performance.
results.evaluation: This finding is presented as supporting the group-level effects at the individual differences level. However, the reviewer's concern about the opposite trend in DAN-A eccentricity compared to group effects raises questions about consistency and interpretation.

results.result: The authors speculate that the relatively small size of the striatum may have limited detection of connectivity changes, as subcortical structures exhibit gradients that may require voxel-level analysis. However, the low-dimensional manifold architecture in cortex did not strongly depend on whether striatal regions were included.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this methodological limitation or the authors' speculation. The null striatal findings are treated as a limitation rather than a fundamental flaw.

results.result: Detailed preprocessing and analysis pipeline: fMRI data were preprocessed using fMRIPrep with standard steps including motion correction, slice-timing correction, coregistration, normalization, and denoising with 34 motion/physiological regressors. Functional connectivity matrices were estimated using Ledoit-Wolf estimator. PCA was used for dimensionality reduction, and individual manifolds were aligned to a baseline template using Procrustes alignment (average r=0.88 correlation). Statistical testing included FDR correction and spatial autocorrelation-aware null models.
results.evaluation: Reviewers described the methods as 'state-of-the-art,' 'convincing,' and representing methodological advances. One reviewer noted the revision 'has produced a stronger manuscript' and thanked the authors for 'thorough responses.' The preprocessing and analysis pipeline is treated as rigorous and appropriate.

results.result: Theoretical framework and interpretation: The authors situate their findings within existing literature on reward-based learning, DMN function, salience/ventral attention network roles in exploration, and the unique topographic position of PMC. They interpret early learning connectivity as reflecting exploration (DAN-salience coupling) and late learning as reflecting exploitation (DAN-DMN coupling), with PMC potentially orchestrating this transition.
results.evaluation: While reviewers found the manuscript 'clear and comprehensible' and the theoretical framing well-articulated, the core interpretive limitation remains: without a control condition, it is unclear whether the observed patterns reflect learning-specific processes or generic attention/engagement dynamics. The PMC interpretation as orchestrating explore/exploit transitions is acknowledged as speculative.

results.result: Overall conclusions: The study establishes neural changes supporting reward-based motor learning and identifies distinct transitions in functional coupling between sensorimotor and transmodal cortex during behavioral adaptation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers described the study as 'valuable,' 'important,' and 'useful,' but consistently noted the limitation that 'it remains to be seen whether these changes reflect generic changes in task engagement during learning or are specific to reward-based motor learning.' The work is seen as motivating future research but not definitively establishing learning-specific mechanisms.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C1-C4 regarding participant recruitment, exclusion criteria, sample size, and ethics approval. Both evaluations find these methodological details standard and acceptable with no concerns raised.

Both address experimental design and behavioral results (C5-C10). OpenEval finds the design well-supported though notes the strong assumption about eliminating error-based learning. Peer reviewers praise the task as 'novel' and 'compelling,' representing a methodological advance. Both accept the behavioral learning effect.

Strong agreement on data preprocessing methods (C11-C18). OpenEval finds the pipeline well-documented with effective centering demonstrated in Figure 2. Peer reviewers praise 'state-of-the-art neuroimaging analyses' and find the manifold approach methodologically sound.

Complete agreement on baseline manifold structure (C19-C24). Both evaluations accept the PCA results, 70% variance explained, and interpretation of tripartite structure as valid foundation. Peer reviewers describe the approach as 'novel' and 'interesting.'

Full agreement on eccentricity metric definition and validation (C25-C29). OpenEval finds the validation approach sound with strong correlations supporting interpretation. Peer reviewers accept this framework without challenge for interpreting connectivity changes.

Both address early learning findings (C34-C37). OpenEval finds results well-supported by Figure 4A with appropriate statistical correction. However, peer reviewers raise critical concern that results could reflect attention allocation or movement speed changes rather than learning-specific effects, marking evaluation as UNCERTAIN versus OpenEval's SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate late learning changes (C39-C41). OpenEval finds the reversal pattern clearly documented and supported. Peer reviewers acknowledge the pattern but question whether changes are learning-specific or reflect generic task engagement dynamics, resulting in UNCERTAIN versus SUPPORTED evaluation.

Both address MPFC seed connectivity (C44-C47). OpenEval finds connectivity patterns supported by Figure 5A with interpretations logically following from data. Peer reviewers praise the seed-based approach as providing 'comprehensive viewpoint' but maintain concern about learning-specificity versus attention effects.

Both evaluate PMd connectivity changes (C48-C50). OpenEval finds the inverse pattern to MPFC well-supported and strengthening overall interpretation. Peer reviewers find the analysis methodologically sound but question learning-specificity, resulting in UNCERTAIN evaluation.
